You click “Run Pipeline,” and then you wait. The spinner turns. Ten seconds. Thirty seconds. A full minute passes before the first task even starts. The logs say “Job is pending,” but the actual delay happened earlier, during “Initialization.” Your massive, multi-template YAML architecture has become a performance bottleneck, and every second of lag is costing your developers productivity and your organization money.

Azure DevOps initialization is not a static file read; it is a complex computation. The orchestrator must fetch every template, expand every ${{ each }} loop, and evaluate every ${{ if }} block to create a final execution plan. For enterprise pipelines with 50+ templates and nested object loops, this “Expansion Phase” can become incredibly slow. “Initialization Lag” occurs when the computational complexity of your YAML exceeds the orchestrator’s immediate processing capacity. This guide provides an “under the hood” look at pipeline performance and provides technical strategies for flattening your YAML to achieve sub-5-second starts.

1. The Anatomy of the Expansion Phase

To optimize your pipeline, you must understand the work the Azure DevOps orchestrator performs before the first agent is even assigned.

Anatomy of the Expansion Phase (The Lag Source)

flowchart LR subgraph Q["1. Queued"] Run["[ Run ]"] end subgraph EXP["2. EXPANSION PHASE (SERVER)"] Fetch["[ Fetch Templates ] (Remote)
[ Expand each loops ]
[ Evaluate ${{ if }} ]
[ Merge Variable Groups ]
(Computational Overhead)"] end subgraph R["3. Running"] Job["[ Job ]"] end Run --> EXP EXP --> Job

1.1: Fetching and Compiling

Every time you use the template: property, the orchestrator must fetch that file. If the template resides in a remote repository or a different Azure DevOps organization, this adds a “Network Tax.” Fetching 20 small snippets across a high-latency connection can add 10 seconds of pure wait time. Furthermore, the engine enforces a hard limit of 100 unique files and 20 levels of nesting to prevent infinite recursion, but even reaching 50% of these limits can noticeably degrade startup speed.

1.2: The Cartesian Product of ${{ each }}

The most significant performance killer is the use of nested ${{ each }} loops to generate jobs or steps. If you iterate through 10 environments, 5 regions, and 4 applications, you are asking the orchestrator to compute 200 distinct blocks of code at compile-time. This Cartesian product directly multiplies the size of the internal parsing memory (limited to 20MB). A pipeline that generates 200 jobs via each will always be significantly slower than a pipeline that generates 200 jobs via a runtime matrix.

2. Measuring the Lag

Before refactoring, you must identify the bottleneck.

2.1: Interpreting the Pipeline Timeline

Look at the gap between the “Queue Time” and the “Start Time” of the first job. If this gap is > 10 seconds and the agent pool is not exhausted, you are suffering from initialization lag.

Diagnostic Step: Check the size of your Expanded YAML. In the Pipeline Editor, select “Download full YAML”. If the resulting file is greater than 20,000 lines, your YAML architecture is too “heavy” for the expansion engine.

2.2: The “Hidden” Fetch Delays

If you use resources: repositories to pull templates from multiple repos, set fetchDepth: 1 and use the 2025 Sparse Checkout feature (sparseCheckoutDirectories) to download only the /templates folder. This reduces the network overhead and speeds up the “Parsing” phase significantly.

3. Optimization 1: Flattening the Tree

A shallow pipeline tree expands faster than a deep one.

3.1: Reducing Recursive Nesting

Aim for no more than 3 levels of template nesting. If a logic block is only used in one place, do not create a separate template file for it. Instead, bring that logic “Inline” into the calling file. The orchestrator processes a single 500-line file faster than ten 50-line files.

Flattening the Tree

flowchart LR subgraph Deep["[ DEEP TREE ]
(10+ Template Layers)"] direction TB Main1["Main"] Stage1["- Stage"] Job1["- Job"] Step1["- Step"] Snip1["- Snippet"] Main1 --> Stage1 --> Job1 --> Step1 --> Snip1 end subgraph Flat["[ FLAT TREE ]
(3 Template Layers)"] direction TB Main2["Main"] Stage2["- Stage (with inline job)"] Step2["- Step (template)"] Main2 --> Stage2 --> Step2 end

3.2: Consolidating Loop Logic

Instead of using nested ${{ each }} loops to generate complex steps, use a single “Preparation” job. This job runs a PowerShell script that parses your configuration and produces a JSON manifest as an output variable. Subsequent jobs then use this manifest at runtime. This shifts the computational work from the orchestrator’s expensive expansion engine to a cheap agent.

The Thin YAML Pattern (The Fix)

flowchart LR Fat["[ FAT YAML ]
(Slow Expansion)
- stage:
each app in 100Apps:
job: Deploy_${app}
(20s evaluation lag)
(100 template fetches)"] Thin["[ THIN YAML ]
(Fast Expansion)
- stage:
job: Prepare
script: parse_apps.sh
job: Deploy
matrix: $(json)
(2s start time)"]

4. Optimization 2: Offloading to Runtime

The most effective way to eliminate expansion lag is to defer decisions to the runtime engine.

4.1: each vs. matrix

The strategy: matrix property is evaluated at runtime and has near-zero impact on initialization speed.

  • Use each only when the structure of the tasks must change (e.g., Job A has 3 steps, Job B has 5).
  • Use matrix when only the values change (e.g., 100 jobs running the same 3 steps with different parameters).

4.2: Dynamic Conditions ($[ ]) vs. Static Checks (${{ }})

Runtime expressions ($[ ]) do not count toward parsing memory or expansion time. Strategy: use ${{ if }} only for structural toggles (like “Include Windows Job”). For all other logic (like “Skip if branch is not main”), use the condition: property.

5. Advanced Techniques: Parameter Pruning

Large object parameters are copied into every template call, rapidly consuming the orchestrator’s memory.

5.1: Avoiding Large Object Payloads

Instead of passing a 50KB configuration object through 5 layers of templates, pass a single “ID” string. Have the leaf template fetch the full configuration from a variable group or a file at runtime. This “Thin Parameter” pattern keeps the YAML metadata small and the expansion phase lightning-fast.

5.2: Conditional Template References

In 2026, you can use ${{ if }} to only include templates that are relevant to the current run. This prevents the engine from fetching and parsing irrelevant files for a specific branch or environment, reducing the total “Include” count and saving network time.

Key Takeaways

  1. Expansion is Computation: Every template and loop has a “CPU Cost” on the orchestrator.
  2. Shallow is Fast: Limit template nesting to < 4 layers to maintain sub-5-second starts.
  3. Offload to Matrix: Shift from compile-time structure to runtime parallelism whenever possible.
  4. Prune Parameters: Keep your object payloads small to avoid hitting parsing memory limits.

This is the last article in the Azure DevOps YAML Expression Masterclass. Return to The Ultimate Guide to Azure DevOps YAML Expressions for the full expression model, or read Expression Security: Preventing Injection and Hardening Your YAML to make your hardened templates mandatory for production.

Sources

  • Microsoft Learn: Pipeline limits and expansion
  • Microsoft Learn: Sparse checkout in YAML
  • Official Blog: Optimizing large YAML pipelines
  • Engineering Blog: The cost of YAML initialization
description: Why large Azure DevOps pipelines take 45 seconds or more to start, what the expansion phase is doing, and how to restructure templates to cut the wait.

Someone on your team runs terraform apply from their laptop. The change goes straight to production. There’s no PR, no review, no record of what changed or why. A week later, something breaks in the landing zone and nobody can explain what happened. You check the Azure activity log and find a dozen manual changes made by three different engineers over the past month — all from local terminals, all with permanent admin credentials stored in .env files.

This is not a process problem. It’s an architecture problem. When your pipeline is “run it locally and hope,” every deployment is a single point of failure.

A GitOps approach fixes this. Every change to the infrastructure is a pull request. Every PR triggers a plan. Every plan gets reviewed before it merges. The pipeline authenticates with a short-lived token, not a stored secret. Nothing reaches Azure without a second set of eyes on the predicted diff.

In 2026, the standard for these pipelines is Workload Identity Federation (OIDC), which eliminates static API keys, and Shift-Left Testing using tools like PSRule. Here’s how to build it with GitHub Actions to deploy Azure Verified Modules (AVM).

1. The PR-Driven Plan-First Workflow

The goal is simple: no change reaches Azure without a human review of the predicted impact. We implement a Plan-First workflow.

PR-Driven Plan-First Workflow

sequenceDiagram participant Dev as DEVELOPER PR participant GH as GITHUB ACTIONS participant Azure as AZURE PLATFORM Dev->>GH: 1. Commit Change note over GH: 2. `terraform plan`
3. [ Resource Delta ] GH->>Azure: terraform plan GH-->>Dev: 4. Post collapsible comment note over Dev: 5. HUMAN REVIEW
6. MERGE TO MAIN Dev->>GH: Merge GH->>Azure: 7. `terraform apply` note over Azure: 8. [ DEPLOYED ]

When you open a PR, the pipeline runs a “What-If” analysis and posts the result as a collapsible comment. Your reviewer sees exactly which resources will be created, modified, or destroyed before clicking merge. No surprises.

2. Secure Authentication with OIDC

Storing AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET in GitHub Secrets is a high-risk legacy pattern. If the secret leaks, an attacker has permanent access until someone notices and rotates it. You probably won’t notice for a while. OpenID Connect (OIDC) solves this by using a trust relationship between GitHub and Entra ID instead of a static credential.

GitHub OIDC Security Boundary

sequenceDiagram participant GH as GITHUB ACTIONS participant Entra as ENTRA ID (AZURE) participant Azure as AZURE RESOURCES GH->>Entra: 1. Request Token
(id-token: write) note over Entra: 2. Validate Subject
(repo:org/repo:environment:prod) Entra-->>GH: 3. Issue Access Token GH->>Azure: 4. Run IaC (Bearer Token)

In 2026, we use Environment-scoped Federated Credentials. This ensures that the production deployment identity can only be used by a workflow running in the production environment branch on GitHub, providing a cryptographic boundary between your dev and prod infrastructure.

3. Shift-Left Testing with PSRule

Compliance should be caught in the pipeline, not in a post-deployment audit. This is the boring part. Do it anyway.

We use PSRule for Azure to validate our Bicep and Terraform code against the Well-Architected Framework (WAF) before it is deployed.

# GitHub Actions: PSRule WAF Compliance
- name: PSRule WAF Compliance
  uses: microsoft/ps-rule@v2
  with:
    modules: PSRule.Rules.Azure
    inputPath: live/

If a developer attempts to deploy a VNet without a diagnostic setting or an unencrypted Storage Account, PSRule fails the build, preventing the non-compliant code from ever reaching the main branch.

4. Safe State Storage Architecture

Your Terraform state files or Bicep Deployment Stacks contain the blueprint of your entire cloud estate. Treat them accordingly.

Safe State Storage Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Hub["[ HUB VNET ] (Management Sub)"] Storage["[ Storage Account ] (State Files)
- Private Endpoint
- Versioning Enabled
- Soft Delete Enabled"] end subgraph Runner["[ SELF-HOSTED RUNNER ]"] MI["- Managed Identity
- (Contributor on Container)"] end Runner -->|RBAC-Only Access| Hub

By using Private Endpoints and RBAC-only access (disabling storage account keys), you ensure that only your authorized CI/CD runners can read or write the state.

5. Bicep Deployment Stacks: The Native Way

For Bicep users, Deployment Stacks (GA in 2025) provide the state management and “Action on Unmanage” features previously only found in Terraform.

az stack mg create \
  --name "lz-management-layer" \
  --management-group-id "mg-platform" \
  --deny-settings-mode "denyDelete" \
  --action-on-unmanage "deleteResources"

The --deny-settings-mode denyDelete flag acts as a native resource lock, preventing anyone (including owners) from manually deleting resources managed by the stack.

6. Separation of Duties: Who Is Allowed to Approve?

A PR-driven pipeline gives you a second pair of eyes. It doesn’t automatically give you separation of duties, and that’s what your change management process will be tested against. The common gap: the engineer who opened the PR is also a repository admin, approves the production environment gate themselves, and nothing stops them.

The setup I’d use has two gates, each with a different job:

  • Pull request review proves someone checked the code. Require review from CODEOWNERS for the platform directories, require approval of the most recent push so a late commit can’t ride an earlier approval, and turn off the option that lets administrators bypass branch protection.
  • The production environment gate proves someone approved the deployment. Add required reviewers, enable prevent self-review so the person who triggered the run can’t approve it, and limit the environment to the main branch.

Put the change ticket number in the PR template. The PR, its review, the environment approval and the run log together form a change record you can hand to an auditor without exporting anything by hand.

What I’d rule out: a single gate where the same group both reviews code and approves deployments. It’s faster, and it’s the first thing an auditor testing separation of duties will find.

Key Takeaways

  1. Two Gates, Two Jobs: PR review checks the code; the environment gate approves the deployment. Block self-approval and admin bypass on both.
  2. Go Secret-less: Use OIDC for all automation identities. Treat static client secrets as technical debt.
  3. Validate early: Use PSRule to catch WAF violations in the pipeline rather than the portal.
  4. Protect the State: Isolate your state storage using Private Link and RBAC to prevent tampering.

Next Steps:

  • Read Cost Governance in the Landing Zone: Tagging Enforcement, Budgets, and FinOps Automation to add cost estimation (Infracost) to your PR comments.
  • Read Day-2 Operations: Maintaining and Evolving Your Azure Landing Zone to implement automated drift detection using these same pipelines.

You need to write a custom Azure Policy that denies any Azure OpenAI resource without a private endpoint. Simple enough requirement. An hour later, you’re still hunting for the right resource provider alias, your JSON nesting is wrong, and the policy ARM rejects on every test run. Azure Policy authoring is a legitimate skill, and the schema is not forgiving. Azure OpenAI can produce a production-ready draft in 30 seconds. That’s not a replacement for understanding what the policy does—it’s a reason to stop wasting time on syntax archaeology.

Azure Policy is the enforcement layer for the entire Privacy-First Blueprint built across this series. Every control—Private Link, Managed Identity, and Zero Data Retention—needs a corresponding policy to prevent configuration drift. In 2026, we are moving toward “Agentic Governance,” where AI agents shift compliance left, auditing Bicep and Terraform templates for gaps before they ever reach the Azure Resource Manager (ARM).

1. AI-Assisted Azure Policy Authoring

Authoring a policy definition requires the correct Policy Alias. To disable public access to Azure OpenAI, for example, you must target the Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/publicNetworkAccess alias. AI models trained on Azure documentation are good at this specific mapping—better than a grep through the ARM provider reference.

Few-Shot Policy Drafting

For the highest accuracy from Azure OpenAI, use a Few-Shot Prompt. Provide the model with correct examples of different policy effects (e.g., Audit, Deny, Modify) to establish the structural baseline.

# Example: Prompt for GPT-4o
"Requirement: Deny any Azure OpenAI resource that does not have its public network access set to 'Disabled'. 
Target Alias: Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/publicNetworkAccess. 
Use 'Indexed' mode and include parameters for the allowed effect."

2. The Policy-as-Code Pipeline

Policies should be managed with the same rigor as application code. A Policy-as-Code repository ensures that every change is versioned, peer-reviewed, and tested before being applied at the Management Group level.

The Policy-as-Code CI/CD Loop

sequenceDiagram participant Repo as GITHUB REPO
(policies/*.json) participant GH as GITHUB ACTIONS
(Validation CI) participant Azure as AZURE MGMT GROUP
(Enforcement) Repo->>GH: 1. Commit Change note over GH: 2. `az policy create`
(Validation Only) GH->>Azure: Validation note over GH: 3. LLM Intent Review GH->>Azure: [ PASSED ] Repo->>GH: 4. Merge to Main note over GH: 5. Deploy Definition
6. Assign Initiative GH->>Azure: Enforce

CI/CD Validation

In your GitHub Actions workflow, use the az policy definition create command in a temporary scope to validate the JSON schema and rule logic. ARM will reject any definition that uses an invalid alias or incorrect nesting—which is exactly the kind of fast feedback you want before a policy reaches a Management Group.

# GitHub Actions: Validate Policy Definition
- name: Validate Policy JSON
  run: |
    # Requires a Service Principal with 'Resource Policy Contributor'
    az policy definition create \
      --name "validate-openai-policy" \
      --rules "./policies/deny-openai-public-access/policy.json" \
      --mode Indexed \
      --only-show-errors
    az policy definition delete --name "validate-openai-policy"

3. Shift-Left: Auditing IaC for Security Drift

Azure Policy is typically reactive—it catches a resource after deployment. Shift-Left Auditing uses AI to scan Bicep and Terraform files in the Pull Request, identifying compliance gaps before they trigger a policy denial.

Shift-Left AI Audit Flow

sequenceDiagram participant Dev as DEVELOPER PR participant Agent as AI AUDIT AGENT participant Policy as POLICY MANIFEST Dev->>Agent: 1. Update Bicep note over Agent: 2. Decompile to JSON Policy-->>Agent: 3. Fetch Baseline Rules note over Agent: 4. Semantic Scan Agent-->>Dev: 5. PR Annotation
(Line-by-line Fixes)

By auditing the semantic intent of the code, AI can catch workarounds—like a developer adding a parameter that defaults to an insecure value—that traditional scanners miss.

4. Explaining Violations in Plain Language

The most frustrating part of compliance is seeing an error like FieldValueMismatch on Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/publicNetworkAccess. You know something is wrong. You don’t know what to do about it.

AI Remediation Guides

Pass the policyState record to Azure OpenAI to generate a fix guide in plain language. The translation from compliance error to actionable instruction takes seconds.

Before: FieldValueMismatch: publicNetworkAccess After (AI-Generated): “Your Azure OpenAI resource ‘ai-prod-01’ is non-compliant. The ‘Privacy-First Blueprint’ requires that public network access be Disabled. To fix this, update line 12 of your Bicep file to set publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled' or run the following Azure CLI command: az cognitiveservices account update ... --public-network-access Disabled.”

This is where AI earns its place in a compliance workflow. Policy authoring is a one-time cost; violation triage happens every sprint.

5. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Integration

In 2026, Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDC) acts as the central aggregator for AI compliance. Use the Custom Recommendations feature to create findings based on Azure Resource Graph (KQL) queries.

// ARG Query: Find OpenAI resources with public access
resources
| where type == "microsoft.cognitiveservices/accounts"
| where properties.publicNetworkAccess != "Disabled"
| project id, name, subscriptionId

6. Where AI Belongs in the Control Loop, and Where It Doesn’t

Every technique in this article puts a language model somewhere in your compliance process. The question your auditors will ask is which steps are controls, and a control has to give the same answer to the same input every time.

The line I’d draw:

  • AI drafts and explains. Policy definitions, remediation guides, PR review comments. A human reviews every draft before it merges, and the policy engine, not the model, does the enforcing.
  • Deterministic tools gate. Azure Policy, PSRule, bicep what-if and terraform plan decide whether a change passes. Their results are reproducible, so you can rerun last quarter’s check and get last quarter’s answer.

What I’d rule out: making an LLM review a required status check that blocks merges. Run the same pull request through it twice and you can get two different verdicts, and you can’t explain to an auditor why a change passed on Tuesday and failed on Wednesday. Keep the AI audit as an advisory comment, and make sure every gap it finds becomes a policy or a PSRule rule, so the next occurrence is caught deterministically.

Key Takeaways

  1. AI Drafts, Engineers Approve: AI handles the syntax; you review the logic. The policy engine does the enforcing.
  2. Shift-Left with Semantic Audit: Use LLMs to scan IaC code in PRs as advisory comments, and turn every gap they find into a deterministic rule.
  3. Audit Mode First: Always assign a new policy in Audit mode for 48 hours to measure impact before switching to Deny.
  4. Policy is the Contract: Your Azure Policy repository is the executable contract for your Landing Zone’s security posture.

This is the last article in the Privacy-First AI DevOps series. Return to The Ultimate Guide to Secure AI DevOps on Azure for the full blueprint and reading order, or read Governance at Scale: Writing and Deploying Azure Policies for the policy-as-code foundation these AI workflows build on.

  • Microsoft Learn: Azure Policy definition structure
  • Microsoft Learn: Create custom security recommendations in MDC
  • GitHub: Azure Policy Community Repository
  • Azure SDK: Microsoft.Authorization policy definitions reference

The Azure invoice arrives on a Friday. $12,000 over budget. You spend the weekend clicking through the Cost Management portal, filter by resource group, filter by service, filter by tag — except half the resources have no tags at all. By Monday you have a spreadsheet, a list of suspects, and a standing meeting that nobody wanted.

“Unlimited scalability” is a great line for a sales deck. It is a liability for anyone who has to explain a bill. The problem is never the scale; it’s that nothing stopped an untagged VM from spinning up at $2/hour and running for six weeks while three teams each assumed someone else owned it.

In your landing zone, cost governance cannot be reactive. If a resource lacks a required tag, ARM should reject the deployment. If a subscription approaches its budget ceiling, your team should know before it crosses, not after. Here’s how to wire up those controls using Azure Verified Modules (AVM) — proactive enforcement and automated anomaly detection, not a spreadsheet you update quarterly.

1. Tagging Enforcement: The Foundation of Accountability

Every FinOps capability — chargeback, showback, and anomaly detection — depends on tags. A resource without a CostCenter tag cannot be mapped to a business unit. That untagged VM from Friday’s invoice? That’s what “no tag” looks like at scale.

Why Tags Drive FinOps

A practical enterprise tagging schema uses 3–5 mandatory keys:

  • CostCenter: Maps resource to a billing entity.
  • Environment: Separates cost by lifecycle stage.
  • Owner: Identifies the accountable team or individual.

Azure Cost Management and the FOCUS v1.3 export format all treat these tags as first-class dimensions.

Proactive Tagging with Deny Policies

A Deny policy evaluates the tags property of an ARM request before the resource is created. ARM will return a 403 Forbidden if the mandatory tag is missing.

Pro Tip: Use mode: 'Indexed' in your definition to ensure the policy skips resources that do not support tags (like NICs or managed identities), preventing “Mystery Block” errors during complex deployments.

2. Automating Tag Inheritance

Your application teams will create child resources — OS disks, diagnostic settings, network interfaces — and those resources will not inherit tags from their parent Resource Group. That’s not a mistake; that’s just how ARM works. A Modify policy closes the gap by automatically copying specified tags from the Resource Group down to every resource created within it.

Tag Inheritance Policy Flow (Modify Effect)

flowchart TD RG["[ RESOURCE GROUP ]
- tag: CostCenter = 'CC-101'
- tag: Owner = 'Platform'"] SA_Untagged["[ STORAGE ACCOUNT ]
- (Initially Untagged)"] Policy["[ AZURE POLICY ENGINE ]
- Action: Append Tags from RG"] SA_Tagged["[ STORAGE ACCOUNT ] (Compliant)
- tag: CostCenter = 'CC-101'
- tag: Owner = 'Platform'"] RG -->|(1. Child Resource Created)| SA_Untagged SA_Untagged -->|(2. Modify Policy Triggers)| Policy Policy -->|(3. Remediation Task)| SA_Tagged

3. Automated Budgeting and Alerts

Every subscription created through the vending process should get a default budget at birth — before any workload lands in it. A $500/month starting budget with notifications at 50%, 80%, 100%, and 110% gives your team escalating signals before spend becomes a Friday problem.

Forecasted vs. Actual Alerts

An Actual alert fires when you have already spent the budget — that’s the financial equivalent of a check engine light after the engine seized. A Forecasted alert fires when the projected month-end cost will exceed the threshold, giving you days to act rather than hours. Make the 80% Forecasted alert your primary operational trigger.

Budget Alert Escalation Path

sequenceDiagram participant UI as Usage Ingestion participant CM as Cost Management participant AG as Action Group UI->>CM: 1. Real-time Metering note over CM: 2. Evaluate Forecasted Spend
(e.g., $410 vs $500 Budget) CM->>AG: 3. [ Threshold: 80% Crossed ] note over AG: 4. HTTP POST Webhook
5. Alert Logic App AG-->>UI: Alert Trigger note over UI: 6. Post formatted card to Teams channel

4. Cost Anomaly Detection

Budget alerts catch predictable overruns. Anomaly detection catches the weird ones — like a developer who accidentally picked Standard_M416ms_v2 instead of Standard_B2s and walked away for the weekend. Azure Cost Management uses deep learning models to distinguish between a legitimate month-end batch spike and an unexpected one. Combined with KQL queries against the Usage table, you can surface “Top Movers” and route them to your platform SREs before the cost compounds.

// KQL: Resource Groups with > $100/day increase
Usage
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize DailyCost = sum(PreTaxCost) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d), ResourceGroup
| serialize
| extend PrevDailyCost = prev(DailyCost)
| extend CostChange = DailyCost - PrevDailyCost
| where CostChange > 100
| project Date = TimeGenerated, ResourceGroup, DeltaUSD = round(CostChange, 2)

5. FinOps Visibility with FOCUS v1.3

Standardize your cost exports using the FOCUS v1.3 format. This normalizes Azure cost data into a cloud-agnostic schema, so your finance team can use the same reporting tools across AWS, Azure, and GCP without manually remapping fields every time someone asks for a cross-cloud cost breakdown.

6. Who Pays for the Hub?

Tags handle workload costs. They don’t help with the line items that belong to everyone: the hub firewall, ExpressRoute circuits, the Sentinel workspace and Defender plans. On a mature landing zone those shared costs can be a large share of the bill, and the first time you charge them back, every business unit will ask why its number is what it is.

There are three ways to split them:

  • Meter actual usage, such as firewall bytes per spoke or log ingestion per subscription. It’s the most accurate, and it means building and maintaining a metering pipeline that finance will still question.
  • Keep shared costs central as a platform budget line. Simple, but it hides the real cost of running a workload and makes the platform team look like the expensive part.
  • Allocate by a published key, usually each business unit’s share of direct workload spend. This is the one I’d pick.

A proportional key is easy to calculate from the FOCUS export, easy to explain in one sentence, and stable from month to month. Finance can defend it, and nobody spends a week arguing about firewall bytes. Publish the key, review it once a year, and start with showback for a quarter before you switch to chargeback, so teams see the numbers before they’re invoiced for them.

Key Takeaways

  1. Tags are the Metadata of Cost: Without enforced tags, FinOps is just guesswork.
  2. Forecast over Actual: Use forecasted alerts to get days of warning instead of hours.
  3. Vending includes Budgets: A subscription without a budget is invisible until the bill arrives.
  4. Audit Mode First: Run your tagging policies in Audit mode for 7 days before switching to Deny.
  5. Allocate Shared Costs by a Published Key: Proportional to direct spend, showback before chargeback.

Next Steps:

  • Read Day-2 Operations: Maintaining and Evolving Your Azure Landing Zone to learn how to maintain these cost controls using automated drift detection.
  • Return to Azure Platform Engineering: The Complete Guide to Building an Enterprise Landing Zone to see how cost governance integrates into the full Landing Zone Blueprint.

  • Bicep Reference: Microsoft.Consumption budgets

Nine months after go-live, internal audit asks a simple question: do the firewall rules running in production today match the ones that were approved? You run terraform plan to prove it. Fourteen changes come back. Three are rule edits someone made in the portal during an incident. One opened a port to a vendor IP range. None of them has a pull request.

Deploying your landing zone was the easy part. Now you have to live with it.

The most common failure mode in platform engineering is not a bad initial deployment — it is treating the landing zone as a finished project rather than an ongoing product. Azure releases new services and deprecates old ones. Organizational requirements change. Configuration drift is not a hypothetical risk; it is a certainty. Without an operational strategy that anticipates these pressures, a well-governed environment gradually becomes a collection of special cases and undocumented manual changes.

1. Managing Configuration Drift

Drift takes two forms: IaC State Drift (code vs. actual resources) and Policy Compliance Drift (actual resources vs. security standards).

Automated Drift Remediation Loop

sequenceDiagram participant GH as GITHUB ACTIONS participant Azure as AZURE PLATFORM participant Issue as GITHUB ISSUES note over GH: 1. Scheduled Run
`terraform plan` GH->>Azure: terraform plan note over Azure: 2. [ Drift Detected ]
(e.g., SKU Change) GH->>Issue: 3. Open GH Issue note over GH: 4. HUMAN TRIAGE
5. TRIGGER REMEDIATION GH->>Azure: Trigger Remediation note over Azure: 6. Policy Fix / Re-Apply Azure->>Issue: 7. [ CLOSED ]

Run drift scans weekly using terraform plan --refresh-only or Bicep what-if. A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow that opens a GitHub Issue when drift is found provides the audit trail and visibility needed for incident response.

2. Remediating Drift Without Downtime

When drift is detected, you must decide whether to import the manual change into your code or revert the resource to its authorized state.

  • Accepting the change: Use Terraform’s import block to bring a portal-made change into your state file.
  • Rejecting the change: Update your YAML/Bicep logic to the desired state and re-deploy.
  • Policy remediation: Use Remediation Tasks to fix auxiliary resource gaps (like missing logs) without touching the primary resource.

The Default Should Be Revert

Importing a manual change is the path of least resistance: the change is already live, nothing breaks, and the drift report goes green. It’s also how an unapproved change becomes an approved one without anyone approving it. Once it’s in your code, the history says it came in through a pull request, and that’s not what happened.

The rule I’d use: revert by default, accept only through a pull request that references the change or incident record that justified it. A firewall rule added during an incident gets a PR within two business days that links the incident and gets a normal review. If nobody can name the incident, the change gets reverted. The drift scan becomes your detective control, and every accepted change has the same approval trail as one that went through the pipeline.

What I’d rule out: auto-importing drift on a schedule. It keeps the plan clean and quietly erases the evidence that the drift ever happened.

# Example: Bulk remediation of diagnostic settings
az policy remediation create \
  --name "fix-logging-baseline-$(date +%Y%m%d)" \
  --policy-assignment "/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-intermediate/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/deploy-vnet-diagnostic-settings" \
  --resource-discovery-mode ReEvaluateCompliance \
  --resource-type "Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks"

3. The Migration Path: Moving to Azure Verified Modules (AVM)

In 2026, the legacy CAF modules are archived. Migration to AVM is a maintenance requirement. A naive migration destroys and recreates resources, but the Terraform moved block allows you to remap the state address without any physical resource impact.

AVM Module Migration (The moved Block)

flowchart LR subgraph State["[ TERRAFORM STATE ]
(Legacy Address)"] Leg["module.enterprise_scale
.azurerm_mgmt_group.prod"] end subgraph Code["[ REFACTORED CODE ]
(AVM Address)"] AVM["module.mgmt_groups_avm
.azurerm_mgmt_group.this"] end Leg -->|"moved (zero destructions)"| AVM

Bicep Pattern: Use Deployment Stacks to manage the transition. The stack reconciles the template change and updates existing resources in-place rather than replacing them.

4. Governance and Identity Lifecycle

The average landing zone accumulates RBAC cruft faster than any other category. Every quarter, your platform team should perform two key reviews:

  1. Orphaned Role Review: Use PowerShell to find role assignments linked to “Identity not found” (deleted) principals and remove them.
  2. Access Review: Use Entra ID Access Reviews (P2) to force on-call engineers to justify their PIM eligibility every 90 days. A “Deny-by-Inaction” default is the safest posture.

5. Hub Evolution: Scaling to Multi-Region

When you expand to a second Azure region, the decision between Global VNet Peering (for simplicity) and Azure Virtual WAN (for massive scale) is your primary architectural pivot. For most organizations, regional hub-to-hub peering is sufficient for up to 4 regions.

# Adding a secondary hub is additive logic
module "hub_secondary" {
  source = "./modules/hub-networking"
  location = "westeurope"
  address_space = ["10.1.0.0/16"]
  peer_to_hub_id = module.hub_primary.vnet_id
}

Key Takeaways

  1. Platform as a Product: Give your landing zone a roadmap and a dedicated maintenance window.
  2. Weekly Drift Scans: Catch deviations in days, not months.
  3. Revert by Default: Accept a manual change only through a PR that links the change or incident record behind it.
  4. Pin Your Versions: Never use latest for AVM modules. Use Renovate or Dependabot to manage upgrades as code.

This is the last article in the series. Return to Azure Platform Engineering: The Complete Guide to Building an Enterprise Landing Zone for the full build order, or continue with The Ultimate Guide to Secure AI DevOps on Azure to bring Azure OpenAI and GitHub Copilot onto this foundation with data controls in place.

  • Azure Verified Modules: Registry
  • Microsoft Learn: Azure Policy Remediation

Your head of platform forwards a one-line email from the CISO: “Can we run a code model ourselves instead of sending source code to a vendor?” You already know the shortlist. You’ve read the benchmarks, pulled a couple of models into Ollama on your workstation, and watched one of them write a decent Terraform module in four seconds.

Then you start drafting the answer and realize the benchmarks cover the part nobody on the approval committee will ask about. They’ll ask who trained the model, under what license, where the weights came from, what happens to the code you feed it, and who can reach the server it runs on. “It scored well on HumanEval” doesn’t answer any of those.

This is the comparison with both halves: which 7B–8B code models are actually good in 2026, and which ones you can get through a security and risk review.

Why the 8B Class Is the One to Evaluate

At Q4_K_M quantization, an 8B-class model fits in roughly 5–6GB of VRAM. That’s the size that runs on a single mid-range GPU, which matters less for a developer’s laptop than for your cost model: one modest GPU server can serve a team, and you can run several models side by side for different jobs.

Below 7B, models degrade noticeably on multi-step logic. Above about 14B, you’re into 12GB+ of VRAM per model and the hardware conversation gets more expensive. The 7B–9B range is where useful capability and reasonable hosting cost meet.

What Actually Matters in Practice

HumanEval and similar benchmarks measure whether a model can write one function from a docstring. That’s a spelling test, not a development workflow. What matters daily:

  • Instruction following: Does it do what you asked, or creatively re-interpret the prompt?
  • Modern syntax awareness: Does it know your framework and provider versions, or generate patterns from three years ago?
  • Context adherence: Does it stay consistent with the files you gave it, or invent variables and imports?
  • Diff quality: Do its patches apply cleanly?

Test models on your own code and your own language versions. Benchmark scores tell you very little about how a model handles your particular mix of frameworks, and nothing about the approval questions below.

The 2026 Contenders

Qwen3.5 9B: The Strongest All-Rounder

Qwen3.5 9B, from Alibaba’s Qwen team, is the most capable general coding model in this size class. It has a 262,144-token native context window (Ollama’s tag lists 256K), accepts images as well as text, and handles multi-language projects well. In practice you’ll run it at 32K context or less to keep VRAM in check, which is still enough for a module and the files around it.

The weights are released under Apache 2.0.

Add explicit version constraints to the system prompt so it targets the syntax you actually use:

FROM qwen3.5:9b

SYSTEM """You are an expert developer. Always use the latest stable APIs.
For Python, target 3.12+ features. For TypeScript, use 5.x syntax.
If you are uncertain about a specific framework version, say so explicitly
rather than generating code that may be outdated."""

PARAMETER num_ctx 32768

ollama pull qwen3.5:9b

Gemma 4 E4B: The Efficient One

Google’s Gemma 4 E4B has 4.5B effective parameters (8B including embeddings), a 128K context window, and accepts text, image and audio input. It’s the lightest model here and runs well on constrained hardware, which makes it a good second model on a shared server: cheap to keep loaded for quick completions while a larger model handles heavier work.

Gemma 4 is the first Gemma generation released under Apache 2.0. Earlier Gemma versions shipped under Google’s own terms of use, so if your legal team reviewed Gemma before, the answer may have changed.

FROM gemma4:e4b

SYSTEM """You are a concise assistant for code completion and small,
well-scoped code changes."""

PARAMETER num_ctx 8192

ollama pull gemma4:e4b

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: The Reasoning Specialist

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is a Qwen2.5 base model fine-tuned on reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-R1. It’s strongest when a task needs step-by-step reasoning: tricky algorithms, debugging logic, explaining why a piece of code behaves the way it does. For routine generation it’s slower and wordier than Qwen3.5.

The weights are MIT-licensed, built on a base model originally released under Apache 2.0.

ollama pull deepseek-r1:7b

IBM Granite 4.1 8B: The Conservative Fallback

Granite 4.1 8B (released April 29, 2026) trails both Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 on real coding work. It has a 131,072-token context window, generates predictable but unremarkable code, and is released under Apache 2.0. It’s on this list because it shows up in every enterprise shortlist, not because I’d pick it.

What keeps it on those shortlists is IBM’s governance story. IBM announced that the Granite 4.0 family was the first open model family certified under ISO/IEC 42001, the AI management system standard, after an external audit of IBM’s training, testing and data governance processes. IBM also says the Granite 4.0 checkpoints on Hugging Face are cryptographically signed. Two caveats belong in your approval memo: the certification covers IBM’s management system rather than the weights, and you should confirm that the 4.1 checkpoints you deploy carry the same signing before you rely on it.

ollama pull granite4.1:8b

Getting a Model Approved

Here’s what your third-party risk, legal and security reviewers will actually ask about each model:

Model Developer Weights license What the reviewers will focus on
Qwen3.5 9B Alibaba (China) Apache 2.0 Developer jurisdiction and provenance; high-level training data description only
Gemma 4 E4B Google (US) Apache 2.0 License change from earlier Gemma terms; confirm legal has reviewed Gemma 4 specifically
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B DeepSeek (China) MIT Developer jurisdiction; trained on outputs of another model; often already on internal restricted lists
Granite 4.1 8B IBM (US) Apache 2.0 ISO 42001 for IBM’s AI management system; signed checkpoints to verify

One point to make early, because it clears up most of the fear in the room: open weights running on your own hardware don’t send anything back to the developer. No prompts, no code, no telemetry from the model itself. The risk with any of these models is about what went into the model (training data, licensing, possible tampering) and about the software around it, not about your code leaving the building.

That reframes the approval. Your reviewers aren’t evaluating a data processor. They’re evaluating a software supply-chain component, and you can treat it like one: an approved source, pinned versions, recorded hashes, an owner.

In a bank, that review usually runs through model risk management as well. US banks working under the SR 11-7 guidance on model risk, for example, will want the model inventoried, its intended use documented and its limitations tested before anyone relies on it. Plan for that paperwork from the start.

Which One to Take to the Committee First

I’d submit Qwen3.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B together, as a pair. They’re the two best models in this class, and they cover each other’s gaps: Qwen3.5 as the primary coder for generation, refactoring and multi-file work, and Gemma 4 as the fast, light model you keep loaded for completions and small changes. One request, one evaluation, one intake process.

Expect them to move at different speeds. Gemma 4 should clear quickly: a US developer, a standard Apache 2.0 license, and nothing unusual for legal to review once they’ve confirmed the license change from earlier Gemma versions. Qwen3.5 is the one that tests your third-party risk team. Some will clear it on the strength of “the weights run offline and send nothing anywhere.” Others have blanket restrictions on models from certain jurisdictions. Find out which kind yours is before you build the pilot, and bring your evaluation showing where Qwen3.5 is materially better on your own code. That’s the evidence that turns a jurisdiction question into a risk decision instead of a reflex.

If Qwen3.5 is blocked outright, run Gemma 4 alone and treat Granite 4.1 as the fallback for heavier work. You give up capability, but you keep the program moving while the Qwen decision is escalated.

What I’d rule out is leading with DeepSeek-R1-Distill. The weights don’t phone home any more than the others do. But DeepSeek’s consumer app has been restricted by several governments and agencies, the name alone tends to stall the conversation, and its strength (reasoning) usually isn’t the bottleneck in day-to-day platform work.

Where It Runs Matters More Than Which Model

You have four realistic options, and the governance picture changes far more between them than between models:

  1. Developer workstations. Easiest to demo, hardest to govern. Every machine has its own model versions, nothing logs centrally, and Ollama’s API has no authentication, so a misconfigured OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 exposes it to the whole network.
  2. A shared inference server in your network. One GPU host or AKS node pool serving the team, with an authenticating gateway in front (Ollama has no built-in auth, so the gateway has to do it), central logging, and one place to pin and update models.
  3. Open models hosted in your Azure subscription. The same as option 2, but on a GPU VM or AKS in a landing zone spoke, behind Private Link, with the identity and policy controls you already run.
  4. Azure OpenAI with Private Link and Zero Data Retention. Not local, but frontier-model capability with network isolation, keyless auth and no retained prompts. See the Privacy-First AI DevOps blueprint.

My recommendation: if your data can legally go to Azure OpenAI under your contracts and classification policy, option 4 gives your developers a much better model for less operational work, and the 8B models become a complement rather than the plan. If it can’t, because a client contract, a data classification rule or a regulator says the code doesn’t leave your infrastructure, choose option 3, or option 2 if you have no suitable Azure footprint.

What I’d rule out is option 1 as the production pattern. Workstations are fine for the evaluation. They’re not something you can show an auditor.

The Decision Matrix

Use case Model Why
General code generation and refactoring Qwen3.5 9B Strongest overall coder; long context for multi-file work
Fast completions on a shared server Gemma 4 E4B Smallest footprint; cheap to keep loaded alongside a larger model
Debugging and explaining tricky logic DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B Step-by-step reasoning, if your risk team clears it
Fallback if Qwen3.5 isn’t approved Granite 4.1 8B Permissive license and governance paperwork; weaker coder

Hands-On: Evaluate on Your Own Code Before You Ask

Your approval request is stronger with evidence from your own repositories than with a leaderboard screenshot. This script runs the same set of prompts against each candidate through Ollama’s REST API and saves the outputs side by side for review.

Put one prompt per line in prompts.txt, drawn from real work: “Write a Bicep module for a storage account with public access disabled,” “Add input validation to this function,” and so on.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run each prompt against each candidate model and save the outputs for review.
set -euo pipefail

MODELS=("qwen3.5:9b" "gemma4:e4b")
OUT_DIR="eval-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR"

n=0
while IFS= read -r prompt; do
  [ -z "$prompt" ] && continue
  n=$((n + 1))
  for model in "${MODELS[@]}"; do
    jq -n --arg m "$model" --arg p "$prompt" '{model: $m, prompt: $p, stream: false}' \
      | curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate -d @- \
      | jq -r '.response' > "$OUT_DIR/prompt${n}_${model//[:\/]/_}.md"
  done
done < prompts.txt

echo "Wrote $(ls "$OUT_DIR" | wc -l) outputs to $OUT_DIR"

Have two engineers score the outputs blind, without knowing which model produced which file. Record whether each output compiles, follows your standards and needed edits. That scoring sheet becomes the “limitations tested” evidence your model risk reviewers will ask for.

Best Practices

Mirror and pin. Pull approved models once, store them in an internal registry or artifact store, and record the model ID that ollama list shows. Production servers pull from your mirror, never straight from the public registry.

Give each model an owner. Someone decides when to move to a new version, re-runs the evaluation, and updates the inventory. “Latest” is not a version.

Keep two or three models, each with a role. One model for everything means picking the wrong trade-off for most tasks.

Verify before you trust a new language or framework. Training cutoffs leave blind spots, and models don’t always know what they don’t know. Send a few representative prompts and confirm the output compiles.

Troubleshooting

Problem: The model consistently generates outdated syntax.

Cause: The model’s training data predates the framework version you’re using.

Fix: Add explicit version constraints to the Modelfile system prompt, for example: "You must use React 19 Server Components syntax. Do not use class components or legacy lifecycle methods." Models follow explicit constraints more reliably than they infer them.

Problem: CUDA error: out of memory when switching models.

Cause: Ollama allocated VRAM for the new model before fully evicting the previous one.

Fix: Unload explicitly with ollama stop qwen3.5:9b, wait for ollama ps to show no active models, then load the next one. On a shared server, size the GPU for the models you keep loaded at once, not for one at a time.

Key Takeaways

  1. Qwen3.5 9B and Gemma 4 E4B are the best models in the class. Qwen3.5 is the strongest coder; Gemma 4 is the most efficient. DeepSeek-R1-Distill reasons well but stalls approvals; Granite 4.1 is a fallback, not a first choice.
  2. Open weights don’t send data back to the developer. The approval question is software supply chain and training provenance, not data egress.
  3. Submit Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 as a pair. Gemma 4 should clear quickly; Qwen3.5 tests your third-party risk team, so bring evidence from your own code.
  4. Where it runs matters more than which model. A shared, authenticated server in your own subscription beats workstations. Azure OpenAI with Private Link and Zero Data Retention beats both when your data is allowed to use it.
  5. Bring evidence from your own code. A blind evaluation on real prompts is what turns a pilot into an approval.
